utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Thursday, October 29, 2009. I would like to first greet all the accused, as well as all the counsels, the Prosecutor, who will carry on her cross-examination, as well as all of the other members of the OTP, as well as all those assisting us. I understand Mr. Karnavas has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Just a brief matter, and I'm speaking on behalf of the Defence teams that have to respond to the 92 bis documentary evidence motions filed by the Praljak team. We are seeking a 15-day extension to respond to that. I did mention it to the Prosecution. I don't know what the exact position is that the Prosecution will take. I understand they may wish to have some additional time as well, but I thought I would raise it at this point because I believe the dead-line is somewhat -- at the end of this week. The documents are rather voluminous, and we want to be rather careful to err on the side of caution, hence this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, all those in and around the courtroom. Good morning. Your Honour, we don't -- the Prosecution has no objection to the request. In fact, I was going to raise this later today. But since Mr. Karnavas is on his feet this morning, let me say, in terms of the 92 bis -- Mr. Praljak's 92 bis filing, the Prosecution has filed its response as of, I believe, yesterday, so that's been filed. However, as to the document motion, the 89(C) motion for the admission of documentary evidence, as Mr. Karnavas has indicated, it's rather voluminous. They're tendering approximately 390 documents, which obviously will take all the parties -- all the other parties some time to review. We would ask to have -- the Prosecution asks to have until the 16th of November to file its response to the 89(C) document motion, but we have no objection to Mr. Karnavas' request. And while I'm on my feet, Your Honour, the other thing -- again, we were going to do this later today, but might as well do it all at one time. In the event that we might, it appears, finish the current witness earlier than perhaps might have been anticipated next week, it would be helpful for scheduling, presumably for the Chamber as well as for all parties, if the Petkovic Defence might indicate whether they would possibly then move the next witness up or if the next witness would still be coming a week from Monday. It would assist everyone in scheduling. If that could be clarified. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning to you and everybody in the courtroom. Our next witness is General Ivan Beneta, an active officer. He has a lot of commitments. He was planned to be here on Thursday and be in the courtroom next Monday. We cannot change our plans, because only yesterday we realised that we might be finished with this witness today. So even if we wanted to very hard, we couldn't bring our next witness any earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. First I'll consult my colleagues for a 92 bis and 89(C) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, you have been translated as speaking about next Monday. I take it that you think a week after next Monday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. I was indeed talking about the week after next, and I believe that the date is 6 November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours -- oh, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the 92 bis motion, of course the Chamber has heard everyone, and authorises the request for the extension of the dead-line, in light of the voluminous documentation to be reviewed. As to the Prosecution's request regarding 89(C), and taking into account the fact that there are 390 documents, the Chamber also authorises the extension of the dead-line and grants the time requested to the Prosecution. The Chamber also notes that General Beneta, who is scheduled for Monday, the week of 9th November, will appear as scheduled on account of his numerous commitments. So no change with respect to the already-indicated Petkovic Defence planning. Mr. Stewart, you're looking at me. Did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just that we've got a general problem here. There are several of us, I don't know how widespread it is, who are simply not getting LiveNote. We've got it on this non-terminal, whatever you call it, but we're not -- we're not getting. So -- and it's that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No discrimination. Same here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm so very glad to hear it. I'm very sorry to hear that Your Honour is inflicted in the same way, but nevertheless relieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The technicians are taking the necessary steps. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and everybody in the courtroom. Your Honours, I would like to seek clarification. I believe that there is a mistake in the record. In your decision, you are talking about extending the dead-line at the request of the parties for submitting a reply to Praljak's submission according to Rule 92 bis. The dead-line was yesterday, if I'm not mistaken, and the replies were already filed yesterday by the OTP, and the Prlic Defence filed theirs two or three days ago. I believe that this should not be part of that decision. We're only talking about extending the dead-line on the documentary motion. Maybe this should be clarified at this point, before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is the motion from 15th of October. We have filed something to the previous 92 bis statements, motions filed by Praljak, so this is related to that particular motion, and I don't see any concern or prejudice to the Praljak team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Chamber, we're talking about the 15th of October motion. Prosecutor, my greetings to you again. I give you the floor for the remained of your cross-examination. I would also like to welcome the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Ms. Alaburic, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gorjanc. Do you have your report with you still? Very good. I just want to review a little bit of what we did yesterday just to make sure that we're all starting on the same page. Yesterday, towards the end of the day, I asked you whether, by your analysis, in the war in the former Yugoslavia no one was a civilian as it related to the All-People's Defence, and your answer was, yes, but there were some caveats for children under 12 and the elderly, with some exceptions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then the second thing that I asked you, which is most relevant, is -- the question was: "So by application, when the HVO made arrests or detained people or isolated people, whether it was a soldier in the field with a gun or, say, a woman in her 20s in her home, it is your opinion that the arrests would have been justified under the All-People's Defence?" And to that, your answer was: "Yes, they would have been justified." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. West. You said, and it's written like this, "by application." You didn't, per chance, "implication"?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, I meant "by application," but I suppose "by implication" would mean the same thing. Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So what I would like to do this morning is look at the documents that support the opinion you gave in your report, and so I'd like to start at the group of people who would be men from 16 to 60. And in your report, at paragraph 14 -- I don't know -- you can go to this if you'd like, but in paragraph 14 you wrote that: "All men liable for military service from ages of 16 to 60 were members of active or reserve forces of the armed forces." Mr. Gorjanc, my question is: What is the source of 16-year-old boys being members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In legal documents, it -- the age of 16 is not mentioned expressly anywhere in the documents. However, following the common practice, for example, in Slovenia, a person could volunteer as a member of the TO once he reached the age of 16. They had to undergo a certain form of training within the TO, and that would have been before they started their compulsory military service. Such practice did not exist in other republics. However, in secondary schools there was a subject called "Defence and Protection" or "Pre-Military Education," for some students even at the age of 16, and for a majority it started at the age of 17 and it was compulsory for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, so that's -- you wrote part of that in paragraph 59 about 16-year-olds in Slovenia, but am I to understand, then, that you don't cite any article of the BiH documents, you don't cite any SFRY article, either, to support the notion that a 16-year-old would be a members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not provided for by the law. However, all citizens who put up armed resistance or any other form of resistance are members of the armed forces, and a 16-year-old could also put up armed -- or, rather, any other resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear, I understand that the way you're coming to the conclusion that a 16-year-old could be a member of the armed forces is the fact that anyone, in any way, could participate to those purposes; it's not because you saw a document that said so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But let's now look at a document. We're going to look at 4D0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I may just ask a question to be more complete. Do you have any document, any article, any source which says that a 15-year-old or a 12-year-old, who puts up resistance, that is to say, throws stones, for instance, therefore would not be also a member of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no explicit legal norm to that effect. That was a constitutional provision pursuant to which anybody who puts up armed or other forms of resistance are members of the armed forces. I must admit that this was more for the political and propaganda purposes than real. That was within the context of the introductory video-clip that depicted Josip Bros Tito, who said that Yugoslavia could arm 8 million people at any one time, could have 8 million people under arms at any one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in paragraph 59, which you were questioned by the Prosecutor, there is a footnote 25 which I've just read, and you mentioned the case of a Slovenian politician - sorry for the pronunciation - Jansa, who has had the rank of corporal as a young volunteer. Is this an example that you mention showing that this man, who had been a young volunteer, so less than an 18-year-old at the time, would have had the rank of a corporal as a young volunteer? I'm just trying to understand this footnote 25. You can take a look at it, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He joined the voluntary units of the TO at the age of 16, in the second grade of grammar school. He was very active in that unit, and before completing secondary education he became a corporal, which would be the -- at that time a rank of an officer rather than of a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So using the example of that politician, what you are saying is that he joined the Territorial Defence at the age of 16? This is the case you mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe that should help the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I would like to go back to the question that Judge Trechsel asked you. It was whether you had seen any document suggesting that a 15-year-old or somebody younger than 16 could be a member of the armed forces. And in your answer, you did mention a document. You mentioned the Constitution; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in your report, the first mention of the Constitution is at paragraph 53, and I'm just going to read the short section from that. Here you write: "Each citizen who participated in the resistance to the enemy with arms, or in some other way, was deemed to be a member of the armed forces of the SFR Yugoslavia." Now, this is from the Constitution of the former Yugoslavia, and you cite Article 240. Now, to focus in on this, the language is "in some other way." Should we understand that the theory you espouse, that people under the age of 16 or people over the age of 60 might have been in the armed forces, is sourced from that language, "in some other way"? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those could be all people who were not members of the TO or military units. It could have also been military conscripts, women in military units, or women not assigned to military units. In any case, this could be all civilians [as interpreted] who were putting up any other form of resistance but armed resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very good. So let's go back to where we left off, and we we're going to talk specifically about the category of people, 16 to 60 men -- 16 to 16 -- excuse me, 16 to 60. And here you do cite a document. You cite 4D01030. So this should be in the binders in front of you, in the small binder in front of you. That's 4D01030.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, just one correction in the transcript. I apologise to my learned friend West. I believe that it will be useful. Page 16 reads that the witness said "all civilians," and the witness said "all citizens." He did not use the term "civilians," but rather the term "citizens."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Gorjanc, this is the Decree Law on Compulsory Military Service. Now, this is the source of information -- and this is for the BH, so it's dated 1992. This is a source of information for when a people would have to go into the obligatory service, and the details that go along with that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. If we can turn to Article 11. In English, it's page 4, but it's Article 11. This is the article you cite in your report, indicating that recruitment for this compulsory military service begins in the calender year where a person reaches the age of 17; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we could go down to Article 13, it's a continuation of that, and it even says in the case of imminent threat of war, that person may be recruited as early as 16; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But if we can just back up to Article 4 a few pages before, I would like to look at that. Article 4, paragraph 3, talks about this recruitment of men for the compulsory military service, but paragraph 3 says: "... citizens of the BH who are fit for military service shall be subject to the obligations ..." Would you agree with me, then, that there's an exclusion here, and this exclusion is people who are sick or unwell or who are otherwise unsuitable for training are not required to do this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And right below that, it says "Chapter 5" in English, but I believe it's Article 5, right below it, it says: "Women shall not be subject to recruitment or the obligation to complete compulsory military service," as well. You would agree that's another exception to this rule?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in your report, at paragraph 102, in regard to this Article 5, you wrote that women can volunteer for training. But, Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me that Article 5 actually limits that volunteering? It says: "In peacetime, military training may be organised for women who volunteer..." So it's only during peacetime that they can volunteer, not during wartime?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So at least from this document, we've now seen that with regard to your conclusion in the report that in practice the entire population served the purposes of armed combat, now at least has some exceptions, and those exceptions, and you can tell me if I'm wrong about this, those exceptions would exclude, for purposes of this document, anyone under the age of 16, it would exclude, for the purposes of this document, anyone older than 60, it would exclude the unfit, and it would also exclude women unless they volunteered during peacetime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Gorjanc, I seem to detect a contradiction between Article 4, second subparagraph, and Chapter 5, which is probably also Article 5, the first subparagraph. In Article 4, it says that: "Female citizens shall be subject to compulsory military service, under the conditions set out in the decree." And then in Chapter 5 or Article 5, it says: "Women shall not be subject to recruitment or the obligation to complete compulsory military service." I wonder whether there is a difference between "women" and "female citizens," or some other explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Women were subject to military obligation, but not to the obligation of being recruited, which was the first level of military obligation. They didn't have to serve in the army as a compulsory service, but they were subject to military obligation from the age of 19 to 50, in keeping with their capability of performing tasks that would have a bearing on the preparation for defence and defence. We have to make a distinction between the obligation to be recruited and a military obligation as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I want to talk to you about a principle of international war of which I'm sure you're familiar, and it's closely related to this idea of being unfit or unsuitable for fighting, and the term is "hors de combat." Are you familiar with that term?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that is? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand the term, it means that the people it refers to are people who are not directly included in combat on the battle-field or up at the front-line facing the adversary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can look at P11072. That is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expert, before we talk about "hors de combat," I would like to come back to the following issue because it's very relevant, in my view, to the issue of minors aged between 16 and 18. I must recognise that until now I had failed to grasp the scope of Article 13 and paragraph 3, and the Prosecutor asked you the question -- a question about it. When you look at Article 13(3), in case of war or the imminent threat of war, the Presidency, and I stress "the Presidency," not "the president," the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina may order the recruiting of persons aged 16. Now, expert witness, can one say that in a particular wartime situation or in the case of an imminent threat of war in the BiH, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a minor aged 16 or 16 and 1 week or half a year could be integrated into the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by a special decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. By this answer, I now ask a new question. From your own point of view, your own point of view, a belligerent party who sees that a soldier from the other party and who is 16 years old and, say, a fortnight, a week, is likely to present a threat, may he arrest him or isolate him in order to protect himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are affirmative, you are positive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to add a question to this. Do you know, Witness, whether a decision to that effect has been taken by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina; namely, a decision that young boys, adolescents of 16 years, have to do compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that, nor was I ever shown a document like that by the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In view of the answer you have just given to the President, do you think it makes a difference for the enemy, in view of boys of 16 years, whether this special possibility to call them to arms has been put into force or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the opposite side was aware of that, because the document was published in the official media, official government papers and gazettes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I find that a bit contradictory, because on line 19-20, you have said you are not aware that such a decision was taken. Now you presume that it is published. How does that go together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we misunderstood each other. I -- what I was saying was that I think that this provision was common knowledge, that it could be taken, a decision like that could be taken, not that it was actually taken. I can't say that it was taken. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And would you then say that the fact that this possibility existed justified the enemy in regarding any way boys of 16 as members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, referring to the provisions of the Constitution whereby each citizen has the right and duty to put up resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not going to discuss this further, but thank you for the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we shall try and conclude on this. During the 10 days' war, Slovenia and -- between Slovenia and the JNA, I shall not get into details, which you know better than I do, but do you know whether the Territorial Defence, which had become the Army of the Republic of Slovenia, had incorporated young boys of 16 or 18 years old -- from 16 to fight against the JNA during these 10 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, and the soldiers who were doing their military service at the time, that is to say, young boys who were 19, did not take part in the war operations. They were removed from the theatre of operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for what reason were they set aside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because on the JNA side in Slovenia, some 2.000 soldiers took part, and on the TO side, there were 35.000 soldiers, well armed and very well trained and highly capable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I understand. Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, just picking up on --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We had the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, picking up on the question posed by the President, during the fighting in Slovenia did the JNA ever make any arrests of people, other than the 35.000 soldiers you mentioned, other people who were in some way -- rather, in an unarmed way supporting the purposes of the Slovenian TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to put something right. The 35.000 soldiers were not captured by the JNA. On the TO, there were 35.000 people taking part, and the JNA did not capture a single civilian or soldier. Over 1.500 members of the JNA were arrested, whereas the others were blocked and held in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gorjanc, and that's my mistake. I didn't intend that understanding. What I'd like to know is whether the JNA ever arrested anyone who wasn't one of those 35.000 soldiers. Did they apply the theory of All-People's Defence, and did they -- in your opinion, would they have been -- would it have been legitimate for them to arrest, again, a young woman in her home who is 20 years old and didn't carry a gun?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but I really think that when examining the witness, we should stick to some sort of order. This is a hypothetical question. It's just like if you asked whether Eskimos need fridges or not. The situation during the war in Slovenia was quite different. The characteristics of that war was quite different from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Slovenia, there weren't three sides, there were just two sides, and the war went on for two days, so this is nonsensical and just a waste of time. It's as if I were to ask the witness what he thinks about a Ferrari, is the back axis too short or whatever, and whether he could apply that to Bosnia. It's a completely unrealistic comparison, and I'm sure you know at least the basics of the disintegration of Yugoslavia within that framework, what the war in Slovenia was like and what its characteristics were, and you cannot compare it to Bosnia-Herzegovina. So to put forward a hypothesis of that nature is absurd. Thank you. I said this to make it easier to relieve my thoughts. Well, General Praljak can suggest something, and why not compare the conduct of the JNA in Vukovar and put forward that hypothesis? But I apologise for taking the floor, but it's just nonsensical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think myself and my colleagues may disagree or not agree with you on everything you've said then; that political situations are different, we agree on that. But Madam Prosecutor, as I have understood, is trying to ask questions on the military plane, and she is starting from an assumption would the JNA, in the fighting situation opposing it to the Slovenian Army, did they arrest people, for instance, women, or not. But the question, which was as -- I asked it myself yesterday. Therefore, it's not a new question. Therefore, it is in military terms that it is asked. The witness has answered, No, so there we are. We don't need to ask for the floor and spend five minutes on this matter, since Madam Prosecutor is asking the military expert a question which is military and which has to do with the behaviour of the JNA. And he is in a position of speaking about the JNA. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned colleague, but since we're dealing with the Slovenian example, and we know a lot of details about the war in Slovenia and that is why it is impossible for us to get to grips with the situation, the basic question was: Did the JNA, in the war in Slovenia, leave the barracks? That's the essential question. Perhaps the witness could tell us something about that, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you have now added to what has been said by Mr. Kovacic, but I don't agree with you. Please continue, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let's go to P11072. It's a small binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask -- this doesn't seem to be in e-court because not all of us have been given binders. We only ever get one set of binders per team, so those of us that don't have the binders are reliant upon the stuff that comes up in e-court. I'm not getting this exhibit. We also still don't have LiveNote, so it's not the easiest morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies to Mr. Stewart. I'm sure it's being up-loaded right now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Stewart, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now my microphone is not working. This is a good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I believe it's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I give up for the moment. It's on now. No, I was going to say I don't know whether I'm the only person who has the handicap on the access to exhibits. I've got a hard copy, so my immediate problem is solved. If nobody else has the problem, we'll end the story, apart from the LiveNote and et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, since there was interruption anyway, I think it is not fair that we are now in trial without transcript in e-court, and this example which my dear colleague Mr. Stewart mentioned also, it doesn't make for us possible to go into the e-court and see the document by ourselves. I mean, it is really difficult. No, we don't have it. No, we don't have it, Your Honour. Nobody here have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could just say it -- to help --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tomanovic, Ms. Pinter, I don't have it. She doesn't have it. Nobody has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just trying to help, Mr. Kovacic. I've found that although the LiveNote is not working, the exhibits could be brought up in the normal way, but this particular exhibit is not there -- oh, it is now, is it? Ms. Winter is very quick with these things, so she's repaired that particular problem. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my associate has just told me that the document that Ms. West called up is on e-court, but under another number. 11073 is the number it's under in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's an obvious solution, then, yes, thank you. Right. Not surprisingly, I went for the number that we were given.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, in fact, it is the number that they were given. There are two documents, 11072 and 11073, that look similar. So if we can go to 11072.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, that's the one I can't get. So 1173 is sufficiently similar, is it, that I can work from there?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if it's not then I've still got the problem. But I've got the hard copy. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The -- in fact, Ms. West, the document under number 11072 that we have in our file here bears, at the bottom, the number P11073, so there is a discrepancy. The paper has a different number, it seems, as compared to the electronic one. But I think everyone has it and we should go forward now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we can all just focus on the ICRC document regarding "hors de combat", regardless of whether it's 72 or 73. Do we all have that? There we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gorjanc, if we could go back to what we were speaking about earlier, which is the principle of "hors de combat," if you look at this document that you have in front of you, this is the Additional Protocol number 1, and it's Article 41, and it says, under number 2: "A person is an hors de combat if: A, he is in the power of an adverse party; B, he clearly expresses an intention to surrender; or, C, he has been rendered unconscious or is otherwise incapacitated by wounds or sickness and is, therefore, incapable of defending himself." Sir, would you agree that a person who is incapacitated by wounds or sickness, and is therefore incapable of fighting, cannot therefore be considered a member of the armed forces, even for the purposes of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we've spoken about, so far, one group of members of the All-People's Defence who appear to be 16 to 60, they're men, and conventionally they would be soldiers on the field, but you write about other groups as well, and you write about five other groups. And let me list those, and tell me if this is correct. These other groups include: People involved in work obligation; secondly, people involved in the civil protection; thirdly, people involved in monitoring or information regarding enemy aircraft; fourth, people who had military training, and, fifth, people who are involved with intelligence, getting intelligence on the other side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so if we were to organise your notion of All-People's Defence, the first group would be the soldiers on the field, and these other people that I've just listed would be those who are unarmed and support the armed forces in other ways; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to talk about each of those groups because I think those groups are the key for the purposes here. And the first are those involved in work obligation, and this is paragraph 72 of your report. You don't need to look at this, but there you wrote: "All citizens capable of working who have turned 15 were subject to compulsory labour service." So under this first group, this would go as young as 15? This is even below 16; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for these questions, I'd like to look at 4D00408. I believe that's in the second binder, the binder in front of you. And this is the decree that you cite in your report regarding work obligation, 4D00408. Would you agree with me, when we're talking about these people -- strike that. If you can go to Article 48, Article 48 of the decree.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see the Croatian text up on my screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you have Article 48?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is the article to which one would cite when they were looking for information about how young you could be for work obligation, and this article says: "All able-bodied citizens older than 15 are subject to work obligation." So, Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me this article specifically excludes those who are not fit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So when you spoke earlier about -- that in practice the entire population serves the purposes of the armed forces, this particular work obligation category is limited to fit people over 15; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not refer to that in the sense of a work obligation -- well, in the sense of work obligation, not in the sense of putting up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. Right now we're speaking just of work obligation. So if we go to your report, in paragraph 72 you list a number of examples of what might be considered work obligation. You list building trenches, building shelters, building obstacles on the battle-fields, building fortifications, building roads. In this paragraph, you don't cite anything. Is this one of those examples of where your knowledge supporting your statement is based on your experience and not based on a document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assertions are based on experience and also on documents, the documents that I received from the BH Army when the population was engaged on trench-building and fortification-building for the needs of the army, and I attach that to my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, you did attach some BH documents regarding this, and we'll talk about those. But in regard to the list, you put a very fulsome list of things and tasks that work obligation would include. You didn't -- you didn't also include a document that supported every one of those tasks that you listed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now I want to go to your experience in Slovenia, because I think that is relevant here in regard to the All-People's Defence. In the course of your experience during the war with the JNA, was the work obligation under the All-People's Defence ever employed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Civil engineering firms, for example, were given the obligation to put up obstructions on the roads against the JNA, and for fortification and other obstructions, but I don't think that there was any strict obligation by which citizens should be rallied together and taken off for work, such as in Bosnia, because there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is that because the war was so short?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So just going to the next paragraph in your report, it's paragraph 73, and you further expand on the types of tasks that somebody in work obligation might do. Specifically, you talk about a delivering and distributing food, providing medical treatment, clearing up the terrain, and then you indicate that work obligation systems could also deliver ammunition and ordnance directly to combat positions on the battle-field. You specifically follow up with: "This task was mostly performed by young or elderly men." Mr. Gorjanc, there's no cite for this, so are we to assume that you've not seen a physical document that would indicate that the young and the elderly were to bring up ordnance to the front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to the second group. We've just talked about the first of five, work obligation. If we move to civil defence or civil protection, which is the second group. It's at paragraph 77 of your report. But you still cite the document in front of you, which is 4D00408, so let's stay with that. But if we can move to Article 71 of 4D00408. It's Article 71 that you cite describing what civil defence is, and this article says: "Civil defence is an all-encompassing organisation, preparing and training citizens, administration bodies, businesses, and other legal entities for participation in non-armed resistance and for protection, rescue, and salvage of people and property from consequences of war, natural disasters, and other calamities." In your report, you indicate that this civil defence in Article 70 applies to citizens between the ages of 18 to 60 for men and 18 and 55 for women; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. West, it is only a question of having the article properly put here. You mentioned Article 71 twice, but actually what you quoted, it is from Article 70, 7-0.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Judge Prandler, thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can move on to the ages, you indicated that it's 18 to 60 for men, 18 to 55 for women, and for that you cite Article 50. So my apologies for making you move around this document, but if we could do that and go to Article 50 of the same document. We see here, under Article 50, it does say men and women, between 18 to 60 for men, and then it says -- at least in my English version it 65 for women, and I assume that's gotta be a typo. But what I'd like to focus on is the beginning of Article 50, it says "all able-bodied men and women." Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me that this group, too, just like work obligation and just like compulsory military service, also has a limitation? It requires that the person be fit in order to be a member of the civil protection; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you see any ABiH documents supporting the theory that they were employing 18-year-olds and 16-year-olds for this type of civil protection?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you see any ABiH documents that support the notion that they were employing civil protection at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any such concrete documents. However, I could see in the media that fire brigades were active, as well as some other services of the civilian defence were also active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expert witness, I would like to tell you that I'm puzzled, not by what you're saying or the questions, but on the topic of civil protection units. Rightly, the Prosecutor stated that in civil protection there could be men and women. All right, this is what Article 50 states. But as far as you're concerned, these civilians in the civilian protection, can they be considered as members of the armed forces under the command of the army, or are we talking about a civil entity under a civilian command; for example, the mayor of the municipality? Could you tell us, these civil protection units, which command authority -- which was their command authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civil protection units were under the command of the civil protection staff that was subordinated to the executive authorities in the territory, either the Assembly or the Executive Board of the Assembly. I can't tell you anything else about the rest of that system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that, in a particular location, women were asked to collect stones and put them on the road - this is just an example - this was not requested by the military authority but by the civilian authority, the municipality or -- requesting this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Work obligation units were activated as part of the authority of the civilian authorities, at the request of the military bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me specify the question. Let's take a theoretical example. Let's imagine -- it must have happened, but I do not have a specific case to mention, but let's imagine there is a group of women placing stones on the road, and they are shot at by the enemy, and a few women get killed. Now, under Slovene law, would these women be eligible for military pension, hence they would be considered as military, or were they considered as civilians and placed under a civilian social security scheme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of fact, they were civilians under work obligation, and their responsibility falls onto those who placed them as a work unit within the reach of the enemy fire, within the fire range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Go ahead, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to the third group that you wrote about, and this would be the group for monitoring and -- the Monitoring and Information Service. It's paragraph 80 of your report, and here you specify that the primary task of this service is monitoring the air-space. And in regard to the decree in front of us, you cite Article 91. At this point, we don't need to go to that, but my question for you is: In this group of your report, you don't cite any ABiH document evidencing that the ABiH were utilising this form of All-People's Defence. Is that because you did not see a document like that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not seen any such thing in any of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we look specifically to your paragraph 81, and I'll just read this out: "These monitoring crews consist of elderly or young persons of both sexes who are not assigned to units of the armed forces or civilian protection units." Mr. Gorjanc, what is your source for that information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source for that information are several BiH Army documents whereby the local population was ordered to provide security for the villages, whereas the local population that was not armed could only carry out the task by way of observing the situation. So they could act as observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you don't even footnote this entire section. It consists of two paragraphs, and there's not one footnote. So these documents that you wrote -- excuse me, you just said the source of that information are several ABiH documents. You don't note them here, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this part. However, they exist in some other parts within that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just so I understand, do you mean they exist in some other parts of the report or they otherwise exist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they exist, and I have noted them in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to belabour this, but can you tell me where in your report you noted those documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'd have to bear with me while I search. One such document is on the following page, 4D01475. You have it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, in fact, we're going to speak specifically about that document, so we can wait a few minutes and we'll get there. But besides that document, is there another one that supports this notion of Monitoring and Information Services?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any such documents, but I base my claim on the fact that the BiH Army engaged population to provide security for the units in the settled areas, and the settled areas themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is that something you took from the media, or how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say it's more from the documents of the BiH Army, reports, orders, and the reports of particular commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move on to the fourth group, and you entitled it "Training and Acquiring Skills for Defence." And that's paragraph 82 of your report. Mr. Gorjanc, I was a little bit confused about this group, because this -- this group talks about people who had training. Are you specifically suggesting that the fact that a group of people had training, but didn't do anything else, was somehow supportive for the purposes of the armed defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, training for putting up resistance, and not only for putting up resistance, but also for protection, for logistics and supply of both armed forces and the population in a war zone, in my view, all that is instrumental to the organisation and putting up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. But if somebody is just trained and they do nothing else than, in fact, just be trained, how is that instrumental to the organisation and putting up resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, amongst other things, they also are trained to put up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, this part of your report is one paragraph long. It's paragraph 82. There are no cites. Did you see any ABiH documents evidencing that they were employing this part of the All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw only the decree law, according to which the right and duty for training for defence is something that has to be done by everybody from the ages of 15 and 65 in order to acquire skills for defence and military training. And when it says "military training," I also imply training for putting up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move to the last category of these unarmed forms of resistance, and this is your paragraph 83, 84, and 85. It's the intelligence activity by citizens. And I'll just summarise, and you tell me if this is right. This is an obligation to provide any information or importance for defence that the citizen might observe or see? It's basically intelligence information; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in paragraph 84, you wrote that the special obligation to which all citizens are subject, regardless of age and sex, so this was sort of like a catch-all group; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be everybody. Everybody could have intelligence. A child could become aware of the imminent approach of the enemy and inform about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm listening to you, and you're saying that even a seven-year-old can provide information. Listening to you, I wonder if, on that basis when there is a war, there are no civilians any longer, only military people, because what can happen? If a warring party realises that the civilian are providing intelligence to the other party, they will deem them or consider them spies and arrest them or even execute them right away. So under that theory, there are no civilians any longer, everyone's a military man; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've claimed that all the while. All citizens have the right and obligation to put up resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to add, that would also apply to disabled persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not understand. Why can't someone who has lost a leg and is walking with a limp and makes observations on enemy movement, why should he not be under an obligation to inform? I see no logic in that limitation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're absolutely right. It was my mistake. My answer was hasty. I spoke too soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You probably thought that the blind man is not obliged to tell what he sees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe -- please don't take this too critically, but it happened yesterday. This is an example of what we mentioned yesterday, that, in fact, Your Honour's question was leading. And I'm not objecting to it being leading, I'm just observing that it is. So when you said, "Just to add that would also apply to disabled persons," it's another example of what we had yesterday. Of course, a witness is going to inclined very readily to agree with such a suggestion put in that form from a learned Judge. It's been cleared up here, but it's just a feature of the way in which witnesses do respond to Judges' questions. But it's not an objection to the form of the question. It's just an observation of the way it works between Judges and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. It's not the first time, of course, that this comes up, and so far Judges have not accepted that their questions must be in a particular form. We take the liberty and ask the questions the way we think is most expedient.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not for me to deprive Your Honours of any such liberty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as we are discussing the further course of the cross-examination, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that there is a difference between the category of an armed soldier and the category of another member of the armed forces who will put up resistance in a different way. The two categories, again, are distinguished from civilians. We all the time are saying that civilians and a member of the armed forces are one and the same, and I believe that this could lead to a major confusion and that at the end of the day we'll not be able to understand what the witness is saying. Let's be very precise, both in the questions and the answers, when we are talking about the categories of the members of the armed forces, whether they are soldiers or other members of the armed forces. That would be all, and that would be by way of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Witness, I wanted to say this to you: When you're asked a question by a Judge, if -- there are five Judges. If I say to you, for example -- if I put to you, There are five of us, don't hesitate to answer, No, no, there's not five of us, there's four of you. So please try and remain independent when asked a questioned by a Judge. I invite you to say "no." It's not because a Judge asked you questions I have to say, Yes, because we really need a contradictory debate. Have you understood my point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I may take a moment here as well. I am certain that Ms. Alaburic's comments were only to make things more understandable and expedient, but I would just caution the Court that any time counsel makes statements of a factual nature, that is not evidence in this case. Now, this is a perfect example where this witness is a military expert about this very question. If there is any confusion, it should be coming from his mouth. Thank you, I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, before we stopped, we were talking about intel information or intelligence information, and paragraph 84 is where you wrote that there is a special obligation to which all citizens are subject, regardless of their age and sex. Now, you do not cite that. Have you ever seen an ABiH document indicating that they employed this part of the All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion is again based on a general constitutional provisional that all citizens participate in resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. At the bottom of this section, it's paragraph 85 where you talk about -- in this case, you talk about neighbours, relatives, elderly persons, women, and even children for information-gathering. You include those groups. You then do cite at this point an ABiH document, and this is the document to which you have referred a couple of minutes ago. So I'd like to go to that document. It's 4D01475. It's in that same binder, the small binder. And you're familiar with this document, sir. This is an order -- an ABiH order to intensify intelligence activities in the 3rd Corps. And if we look at that document, I think what you were focused on was number 2, which is: "Engage the intelligence organs primarily in organising and gathering of information on the aggressor's forces, activities, and intentions. And as a special task, maintain connections with our structures and sympathisers in temporarily occupied territory." Mr. Gorjanc, this word "sympathisers," is this the source of your information that neighbours, relatives, elderly persons, women, and even children were used for information-gathering? Are those the people that you would consider sympathisers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not only on that. That's just one of the documents. This document doesn't specifically talk about sympathisers, it doesn't say whether it is men, women, younger or older people. I base my conclusions on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I want to make sure I understand. You just said that it's not only that document, that's just one of the documents. So presumably you mean that there are other documents, but when you look at this section of your report, you only cite that document. Are you suggesting to the Trial Chamber that you base your opinion on other documents that you do not cite in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cited almost all documents that the Defence had made available to me. However, I did not deem it relevant to cite all the documents in every place. I am not a legal professional and I didn't know that I should corroborate each and every claim of mine by a document. I believe that most of the claims are widely known, at least to us in the former Yugoslavia, and that most of them do not require any particular additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so let's just look at your answer. You just said: "I cited almost all documents that the Defence made available to me." So are we to understand, when we look at your report and we look at the footnotes, almost all the documents that the Defence gave you to review in support of your theory are cited?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, therefore, the only document in this entire section of these five -- these five groups that we've been talking about, the work obligation, civilian protection, training, monitoring of aircraft, and intelligence work, the only document that I can see from your report that could involve elderly or women or children is this document, 491475? So is this the document upon which you base your theory that women, children, elderly are part of the All-People's Defence ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That document confirms only the fact that all citizens were duty-bound -- or, rather, that they were reckoned with when it came to intelligence activities on behalf of the armed forces or, rather, the BiH Army. Other claims are corroborated by other documents which I cited elsewhere when I spoke about other things. As far as I know, the engagement of work obligation units, as one part of this chapter, has been confirmed by two different documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this might be a good place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In connection with the issue of documents that you have based your report upon, I would like to know whether you had documents from other sources than the Defence or whether you, yourself, went out to investigate documents that you thought might be useful for the fulfillment of your task.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first part, or especially All-People's Defence in the former Yugoslavia, I had my own documents. However, when I was asked about the doctrine of All-People's Defence in the territory in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I asked for additional documents, which the Defence provided. Other documents, reports, orders, and other such documents is something that I was able to find on the web pages of General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it would be useful for the witness to tell us how many documents there are on General Praljak's web pages. This would give you an insight into that database, and you would then be able to qualify this statement about the source of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer. I did not count them, but I know that I was perusing the site for weeks. I was maybe even -- I would maybe glance at some of them to see whether they were relevant and move on. I believe that there were over 20.000 documents, all in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for the break. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We resume. Mr. Scott, a specific point. A while ago, when you asked extending the time for the motions, 92 bis, in fact there have been three motions. The first concerns the admission of 155 declarations, and this is dated 14 September 2009. We have also 22 -- we had given an extension on 22 September for until the 28th October. And concerning this motion, which Petkovic, Prlic and Pusic Defence also filed their motions, and apparently yourself too, this is the first motion. The second has to do with the admission of four statements, 92 quater, and the time to answer was 28 October, and you have filed your response yesterday. And the third one is the request from the Praljak Defence concerning the admission of evidence -- documentary evidence, instead of the deposition of Vlado Djuric under 92 bis, and this is a motion of the 16th of October, with the possibility of answering the 30th of October. And to date, only yourself have filed a response. So, Mr. Scott, when you requested an extension, for which motion was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The request that we made was in response to the documentary motion. Mr. Praljak's Defence has recently filed a motion to admit 390 documents by motion. That is the document -- excuse me, the motion upon which we request an extension to the 16th of November. The Prosecution has responded, so far as we know, to all pending 92 bis motions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this was a request for extension concerning the motion concerning Directive L-9. That's it, very well. So now everybody's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now everything is clear. And if I may so, as a moving party in the case of documentary motion, we do not certainly object on the Prosecution request to response, because we were in the similar situation in the Prosecution case and we were also granted a longer time. I don't remember how much, but considerably, but it is work -- it is a lot of work. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now we have clarified this problem. Therefore, we shall now proceed, and, Ms. West, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, before we stopped, we were -- you had mentioned that you took about two weeks and you looked at the Praljak web site and there was 20.000 documents, so you have perused --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a correction. The witness didn't say "two weeks." He said "for weeks and weeks," which in our language means many weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very good. So many weeks, lots of documents. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So my question is: Of all the documents you saw, would you agree with me that it would make sense to put the best documents that you saw, the best documents that supported your theory, in your report? It would make sense to put the most persuasive documents in your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, in fact, you did that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so just so that we're clear, as to these five groups we talked about of unarmed resistance, as far as I can see, there are four documents that you cite, four ABiH documents. I'm not talking about decrees or anything, but factual ABiH documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's move on, Mr. Gorjanc. I want to turn our attention to some HVO documents, because I understand that in your report you did not include any HVO documents. And I want to look at them to understand whether -- whether they may -- whether they relate or they don't relate to the theory that you've presented to the Court. So the first document is P03133, and I believe it's probably in the bigger binder, the first big binder. 3133. And, sir, this is a July 3rd, 1993, document. It's a report about the Heliodrom, and it talks about the people at the Heliodrom and what was going on there. But specifically if we go to the second page in English, and for B/C/S it's the one page, it's the paragraph that begins with: "Checklists of persons younger than 18 and older than 60 have been made. They will be sent home with the consent of the Department of Defence." And then it indicates that this is 82 people. Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me that if these 82 people were sent home, just assume this document to be factually correct, they were sent home, they were likely not supporting the BH armed forces and were civilians, because otherwise they would not have been sent home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we'll move to the next document. It's P03344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, this document says these persons will be sent home. You have been asked whether they actually were sent home, and you said, "Yes." How do you know that they actually were sent home? Do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at the answer, the answer was not whether they were sent home. He's not validating that. He's validating the reasons why they would have been sent home, if I'm -- if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, "otherwise they would not have been sent home," is what I read. This clearly implies that they were, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure that this is my inelegant question. I think Mr. Gorjanc and I understood each other, but my question was: Assuming they were sent home, so assuming that factual premise, they were sent home because they were civilians and not otherwise supporting the armed forces? And the answer was, "Yes." And so let's just do that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is your answer supporting my conclusion that they were sent home because they were civilians and not otherwise supporting the armed forces, not that they were sent home?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for being meticulous. I sometimes am.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Of course. So if we could move to 3344, P03344. This is a July 9th document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what I'm going to do is the same thing that Ms. Alaburic did. I'm going to show you a number of documents. I want you to assume them to be correct, and then I will ask your opinion about them. So I'm not asking you factual questions. Just assume factually this is the correct information. I'm only asking for your opinion about these documents. In this document, this is a list of persons detained at the Heliodrom who were interrogated, and there's several people listed here. And as you go through them, for example, number 2, at the bottom of number 2, it says -- whoever wrote this, this HVO person who wrote it, labelled them a civilian. Number 4, that person was born in 1932, so is fairly old; also labelled that person, at the end of the sentence, as civilian. Number 5 is labelled as civilian. Go to the next page. I can quickly see that 7 is a civilian, 10 is a civilian, 11 is a civilian, 12 is a civilian. We get to 15; civilian as well; 16, civilian; 17, civilian. I'm going to stop there for a moment and focus in on 15 and 17. In these two cases, it indicates that these people -- 15 is -- had work obligation in the mine of a dark -- in the mine -- a coal mine, "was a civilian," and 17, the last sentence is: "He fulfilled his work obligation in the project, was a civilian." My question, Mr. Gorjanc: Is it possible to be both, to be somebody who has a work obligation but also to be a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a matter of interpretation, because if a person has a work obligation and is subject to work obligation, it's included in one way or another into the defence system. He's not a classical civilian, whereas here these people are being classified as civilians. Probably the notion of civilian here applies to somebody without weapons and not having been deployed in a unit, whether it be a BH Army unit or an HVO unit. So in that context, he would be a civilian. That's the understanding of "civilian" here, and that's how we understood it. However, in legal terms, once again, following the constitutional provision and legal provisions on All-People's Defence, in actual fact every member is subject to work organisations and, as such, was a member of the armed forces; not a member of the army, the HVO or whatever, but a member of the term "the armed forces." That is what the laws dictate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expert witness, you are now putting us in a form of confusion. It's difficult to follow you, and I'm going to explain why things are getting confused. Starting from the document we have here, where one sees some people who are considered as civilians, let's say number 17, who had a work obligation in the Projektant, you say that since he has a work obligation, he is in the armed forces, because you refer to the concept of All-People's Defence. Now, let's consider a civilian, a plain civilian, whoever, a lady, a woman, and under the terms of civilian protection she's going to be asked, after a battle, to go and get the corpses, because the battle-field has to be cleared, and also, therefore, to take the killed soldiers, and she does so. She takes the bodies away, which are going to be transferred to the morgue and to a cemetery and so on. Is she a part of the armed forces? Because at the end of this work she is going to go back home and look after her children, and you say, no, she is within the armed forces, and there I just don't understand. What do you mean, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the law deems everybody who puts up an armed resistance or resistance in any other way to be a member of the armed forces, but not a member of a unit. So following on from that legal provision, we can consider everybody who contributes to the defence is a member of the armed forces. The law also stipulates that all members of the civilian protection system have equal rights as are enjoyed by members of the armed forces, that is to say, members of the army, and all conscripts of work organisations, while they're doing their work assignment, enjoy the same rights that soldiers do in their units. So in that context, too, we consider those civilians to be, in a way, members of the armed forces, as a broad term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take an example. Imagine, in Mostar, that the wife of a military of the HVO, who is a mother with four children. Then the municipal authority tells her, Madam, you're going to retrieve bodies because there have been artillery shelling and we need people to go to mop up the battle-field. So this lady leaves her children and goes to get the bodies. Then she comes home and she starts looking after her children. If I understand what you say, you consider that this woman is integrated in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, yes. However, I have to say that women with children under the age of seven were not subject to military obligations, and these were the bylaws. This was stipulated in the bylaws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Therefore, for you, everybody is in the armed forces. This is the conclusion which you give us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expert witness, you just said also that any person who opposes an armed resistance or any form of resistance, in English, "any other manner," a member of the armed forces. Could you give me an example of any form of resistance, other than armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That might entail putting up obstacles along roads used by the enemy, by cutting down trees and placing logs across a road or large stones, and so on and so forth, or inflicting direct harm and damage to military installations or vehicles. It can also be propaganda activity, for example, by handing out pamphlets against the enemy, or any other form of activity, for that matter, which will affect the combat readiness of the adversary, of the enemy, and will affect the enemy's morale, designed to undermine enemy morale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, several times you use the word "resistance," because you start from a premise which is that all citizens are resistance -- are resisting. But in the case of the woman which I gave you as an example a while ago, whose husband may be in the HVO, it would be the same for the ABiH. Her only problem is to look after her children in her own life, but she's being requested to do this job, and then after that, once it's done, she goes to look after her children. Military or political problems, she's not concerned. And despite this, you consider that she's a resistant, unwilling resistant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a way, that particular woman would be supporting the armed forces because, as the task you've quoted, otherwise they would have to involve soldiers from the front-line and take them away from the front-line to perform the tasks she was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We're going to reflect on all this. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, and I apologise to my colleague, as soon as this document came up, because I would like to indicate something that is illogical in this document, which would take us down the wrong path. At the beginning of the document, and this was read out by my colleague, it says that this is a list of persons who were interviewed on the 9th of July, 1993. Now, if we take a look at the person under number 17 that we looked at just now, in that particular paragraph it says that he was included in the Rama Brigade until the date stipulated here, and then at the end of the text it says "civilian."
